I know this may sound shocking to you seeing that most conservatives and progressives are opposed to an internet sales tax. The logic being that it is the internet and is not located in one state and therefore needs to be tax free. Which, you know, does have it's merits and is a solid argument against internet taxing.

However, out of the 51 sovereign states all but **five ** have some sort of internet sales tax or a use tax. Go a head a check it out here Guide

Now, you may be saying to yourself that it cant be true because you have never payed tax for internet purchases. However, that is because that companies only collect tax on their sells if they have a presence in the state that they buyer is in. Meaning that if you buy something from a company that has zero presence in your state than the state it the one that collects the tax. However, by law you do need to declare your internet purchases when you pay tax or how ever your state collects it.

So, now that I have made it clear that 46/51 states have a use tax I will tell you why it is much simpler to have a national internet sales tax.

  1. There would be little confusion as to what tax you pay and who collects it(The state or the company)
  2. It would lower the operating costs of who ever is the collector.
  3. State budgets would be easier met it the use tax is collected.

Now some more serious reasons.

  1. A national tax would save thousands of jobs. Let me explain, with the current scenario many companies are being forced to fire employees located in other states to get rid of the presence there. A great example of this is what happened with Amazon and my state of Colorado. Amazon had been using affiliates to advertise their products. Which was not a presence because they were not direct employees. However, Colorado passed a bill that made them employees in order to close a budget shortage. Amazon had two choices, either spend tons of money and collect taxes for Colorado or cut ties with the affiliates. Like any sound business would they made the hard choice and were forced to fire all of their Colorado affiliates. Story Many more if you google it

Keep in mind this also happens as a small business level as well. My summer work had to let someone go for a similar situation.

  1. The lack of a national tax makes it easy for large states to extort money from small businesses. My summer job was dealing with a situation involving this. I dont want to use any specifics because I dont want to hurt my work. A very large state was dealing with a massive budget shortage and needed money. They could collect the taxes from it's citizens and stores but that would cost a lot of money that they did not have. So, they went after a lot of small businesses. Lets say I have Small business Aplha or A. A is located in Main and makes a lot of sells to New York. A does not need to collect the taxes for New York because A does not have a presence there, and only has a small office in New Jersey. However, one year New York quietly changes it's law making the office in Nee Jersey a presence in New York because the people take clients to lunch in New York.(Really any loophole works if it is secret)

New York now has a solution to their budget problems. They go to the company in Maine and tell them the law changed and they give them a bill of all the taxes to collect or pay themselves. The company in maine now has to hire people to track down all of the customer in New York and have them pay the use tax. It is impossible to track down everyone so in the end the maine company ends up paying the difference. New York does this to a hundred Maine companies at say 30,000 a piece and their budget shortage is now not looking that big. They also know the small businesses have no manpower or capital to fight it in court and it is just cheaper to pay the fines. Thus legal extortion.

  1. These small businesses have to comply or they get a "random audit" by the large state,

  2. People are not aware of the use tax and that is where the problem starts. Lets say you are working as an intern for a bank and you boss gives you his company credit card and tell you to buy office supplies. You makes the purchases, but you would not think to declare the use tax or you might even be gone by the time tax day comes.And thus, your state now has a method to extort money from the office supplies company.

To sum it up, use tax all ready exists. However each state having their own system creates a nightmare for workers, small businesses, and state governments.

A couple of questions:

Are you advocating a federal level sales/use tax system. (seriously, you want the Fed's to build a giant "IRS" like bureaucracy?)

Are you aware that the 'use' tax is poorly enforced by states for a reason?

(during my early career, I had business clients who were subjected to state use tax audits - so, while I can't claim knowledge of all state's differences I do have a very large body of information on how these taxes work.)

Simply, tax laws require enforcement. I have never heard of any tax system that was successful using the honor system.

Background: We have all paid "sales taxes" on taxable goods that we have purchased. Use taxes are an attempt to "balance" the rules so as not to create an advantage against "brick and mortar" stores. They aren't a new thing and it has been my experience that enforcement by states is limited to businesses making large purchases of personal property that will not be resold to customers. (Example: Tax cheats 'r' us, inc. decides to refurnish the corporate offices with new furniture for every employee. Being wise consumers, the furniture is ordered and shipped from a company that does not have "nexus" - brick and mortar sales location in that state. Under state's use tax law, the business is still required to file a use tax return and calculate/remit the amount of local sales tax that would have been paid had the business purchased locally.)

Technically, the law applies (there are differences among states) to individuals. However, I have never heard of an individual being subjected to an audit. (think about it, that gift you bought in St. Louis but had the helpful storekeeper ship it to your home in southern Illinois will have avoided Missouri state sales taxes). The most common exception to not enforcing the use tax on individuals is when you purchase a vehicle out of your state. I believe that all states "catch" you when you go to register the vehicle in your home state. If the tax paid at to the dealer in the selling state is less than the tax you would have paid in your home state, you have to pay the difference.

Advocating that the Fed's or individual states should "gear up" and enforce this type of tax is unworkable. The manpower requirements alone would be more than the taxes collected.

Further, this issue existed before the internet - youngsters, go ask your grandparents about something called a mail-order catalog. If confused, ask them to tell you about the US postal system....

(phew, this is why I left being a tax accountant many years ago, the rules have to be incredibly detailed in order to be enforced)

Last thought - I am assuming that you realize that sales/use tax are what is referred to as "regressive" taxes - the revenue collected ends up being disproportionately born by lower income households (the ratio of tax paid compared to total income)

Rather than advocate for a new federal bureaucracy, why not advocate to abolish all sales/use taxes and replace with income taxes based on more graduated tax rates. Properly enforced, income taxes share the cost of government "fairly" based on a percentage of your income and not "unfairly" as a percentage of what you buy.

(Side note: all successful businesses that I have knowledge of always try to find ways to lower costs, sales taxes are a cost - it costs money to be able to account for and collect sales taxes - to some businesses. You should ask yourself why is a tax levied on "goods" and not services?)
